title: Why Data Travels in Packets
about: Why your data is cut into small pieces before it travels.

cards.prompt: Someone at home is streaming a film while you play an online game, on the same Wi-Fi. Imagine the film was sent as **one giant piece**, all in one go. What would happen to your game meanwhile?

options.text: Your game would freeze, waiting until the whole film had finished arriving
Nothing changes: the Wi-Fi would carry the film and the game side by side
options.nudge: One giant piece takes up the whole connection until it's done. Could anything else squeeze past it in the meantime?

options.text: Your game would run faster, because the film would be out of the way sooner
options.nudge: The film isn't out of the way while it's still arriving. Think about your game's data while that giant piece is on its way.

options.text: The TV would cut the film into pieces itself, so the game wouldn't notice
options.nudge: In this question the film is sent as one giant piece, and the TV only receives it. What happens to anything else that needs the connection?

cards.explanation: One giant piece would hog the connection, so your game would have to **wait** until the whole film had arrived. That's why the internet never sends data that way. It chops everything into small pieces that take turns, so both the film and the game keep going.
cards.hint: Picture one enormous lorry blocking a single-lane road. What happens to the small cars behind it?

cards.title: Numbered postcards
cards.body: So the internet chops data into **packets**: small pieces that **take turns** on the connection. Each is like a numbered postcard: some data (the **payload**) plus a label with the **source** address (from), the **destination** address (to) and, for most data, a **sequence number**. With the rules called **TCP**, a lost packet is sent again on its own.

cards.prompt: Here's one [[packet]] from a selfie you're sending. Match each part to what it's used for.

pairs.right: Where the reply goes back to
Where it fits when the selfie is rebuilt

pairs.left: A strip of the selfie's pixels

cards.explanation: **From** is the source address: the device that sent it, so that's where any reply goes. **To** is the destination address: where the packet is heading. **#3** is the sequence number, so the selfie can be rebuilt in order. And the strip of pixels is the **payload**, the actual data.
cards.hint: Think of the numbered postcard: who it's from, who it's to, its number, and the bit of the story it carries.
cards.nudge: A reply goes back to whoever sent the packet. The number is only about putting pieces back in order.

cards.prompt: A message is **6,000 [[bytes|byte]]** long. If each [[packet]] carries exactly **1,500 bytes of data**, how many packets are needed?
cards.explanation: 6,000 ÷ 1,500 = **4** packets. In real [[networks|network]], the label (addresses and so on) uses up a little of each packet's space, so each one carries slightly less data and this message would need one more packet.
cards.hint: How many 1,500-byte loads fit in 6,000 bytes?
cards.nudge: Each packet carries 1,500 bytes of the message. How many lots of 1,500 make 6,000?

cards.prompt: Put a message's journey in order.

items.label: The message is split into small pieces
Addresses and a sequence number are added to each piece
The packets travel across the network
The receiver uses the sequence numbers to rebuild the message

cards.explanation: The data is **split** first, then each piece gets its **addresses and sequence number**, which turns it into a packet ready to travel. The receiver can only rebuild the message once packets have arrived, using the sequence numbers to put them in order.
cards.hint: Something has to exist before it can be labelled, and a message can only be rebuilt once its pieces have arrived.
cards.nudge: The addresses and sequence number are added to each piece, so the pieces must exist first. Rebuilding happens at the very end of the trip.

cards.prompt: So why does the internet split data into [[packets|packet]] instead of sending it as one long stream?

options.text: Conversations can share the connections, and with TCP a lost piece is resent alone
Splitting data into pieces makes the files smaller, so they travel across the internet faster
options.nudge: Splitting a file into pieces doesn't shrink it. Each piece even gets a label added, like addresses.

options.text: Splitting data up keeps it secret, because nobody can read just one small piece
options.nudge: Anyone who collects all the packets can put them back together, so splitting doesn't hide anything.

options.text: Cables can only carry one letter at a time, so big files have to be broken up
options.nudge: Cables aren't limited to one letter at a time. Think about the film and the game sharing the Wi-Fi.

cards.explanation: Packets let lots of conversations **take turns** on the same connections, and with TCP, if one goes missing, only that piece needs sending again. Splitting doesn't make data smaller (the labels actually add a little), and it doesn't hide anything: anyone who collects the packets can put them back together. Keeping data secret is a job for **encryption**.
cards.hint: Think back to the film and the game sharing the Wi-Fi, and what happens when one piece goes missing.

cards.prompt: You're downloading a file split into 10 packets, using [[TCP]] rules. **Packet 7** gets lost on the way. What happens?

options.text: The receiver spots the gap after 6, and only packet 7 is sent again
The whole file is sent again from the start, because one piece is missing
options.nudge: The other nine packets arrived safely. With packets, only the missing piece needs sending again, not the whole file.

options.text: The file arrives with a hole in it, and nobody notices anything is wrong
options.nudge: The sequence numbers show a gap between 6 and 8, so the receiver can tell something is missing.

options.text: The download stops for good, and you have to start it again yourself
options.nudge: One lost packet isn't the end. Think about what the sequence numbers let the receiver notice and ask for.

cards.explanation: Thanks to the sequence numbers, the receiver can see there's a gap between 6 and 8. Under TCP's rules it tells the sender, so **packet 7** is sent again. The other packets already arrived safely, so there's no need to start over.
cards.hint: Each packet carries a [[sequence number]]. What could the receiver notice when number 7 never turns up?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Data travels in small pieces called **packets**.
- Each carries data plus addresses and a **sequence number**.
- Packets take turns; with **TCP**, a lost one is resent alone.
